2026-07-01 10 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Adobe has released patches for multiple maximum-severity security flaws impacting Adobe ColdFusion and Adobe Campaign Classic. The ColdFusion updates "resolves critical and important vulnerabilities that could lead to arbitrary code execution, privilege escalation, arbitrary file system read, and security feature bypass," Adobe said in an alert released Tuesday. The vulnerabilities are listed

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Adobe ColdFusion / Campaign Classic hosts exposed to APSB26-68 CVSS 10.0 RCE CVE · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Path-traversal / dangerous-upload exploit requests to Adobe ColdFusion & Campaign Classic endpoints (APSB26-68/71) · [LLM] Adobe ColdFusion / Campaign Classic service spawning a command interpreter · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Web shell written to web root by ColdFusion / Campaign Classic runtime · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Path-traversal / dangerous-upload exploit requests to Adobe ColdFusion & Campaign Classic endpoints (APSB26-68/71) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests carrying directory-traversal sequences or hitting ColdFusion/Campaign admin-and-upload endpoints, matching the unrestricted-upload (CVE-2026-48276/48283), improper-input-validation, and path-traversal (CVE-2026-48282/48313) flaws Adobe patched. Article-specific because it keys on the exact ColdFusion (/CFIDE/, /cf_scripts/, *.cfm/*.cfc) and Campaign Classic (/nl/, /nms/) request surfaces. Rationale: Uses the exact ColdFusion (/CFIDE/, /cf_scripts/, .cfm/.cfc) and Campaign Classic (/nl/, /nms/) request surfaces plus encoded-traversal tokens tied to CVE-2026-48282/48313; defender/falcon/datadog left empty because IIS/web-request URIs are not carried in Defender AH, FDR, or the listed Datadog sources. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seo-poisoned-software-sites-abuse.html • https://helpx.adobe.com/security/security-bulletin.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1083 T1005
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ColdFusion admin UI navigation that URL-encodes path segments
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Burp) probing /CFIDE/ with traversal payloads
  • Web app that passes relative paths in query strings for template includes
  • Search-engine crawlers hitting stale .cfm links resolved via rewrite rules
  • Load-balancer health checks appending encoded path fragments
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has "Nessus" and csUserAgent !has "Qualys" and csUserAgent !has "Burp"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the source IP's full request timeline; confirm whether the traversal token returned 200/500 (successful read/exec) vs 403/404 and whether the IP is an approved scanner. Step 2 (contain): If a 200 to a sensitive path (web.config, datasource creds, /etc/passwd) is seen, block the source IP at the WAF/firewall and isolate the ColdFusion/Campaign host pending patch to ColdFusion 2023 U21 / 2025 U10 / ACC v7 7.4.3 build 9397. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to the same host's process and file telemetry for interpreter spawns or new .cfm/.jsp web-shell writes following the request.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/CFIDE/", "/cf_scripts/", "/coldfusion/", "/nl/", "/nms/") or csUriStem endswith ".cfm" or csUriStem endswith ".cfc"
| where csUriQuery has_any ("../", "..%2f", "..%252f", "%2e%2e", "..\\") or csUriStem has_any ("../", "%2e%2e")
| summarize Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Methods = make_set(csMethod), Statuses = make_set(scStatus), SampleQuery = any(csUriQuery) by cIP, csUriStem, Computer, csUserAgent
| order by Hits desc
title: Directory Traversal Against ColdFusion / Campaign Classic Endpoints
id: 8f3d1c22-6a4e-4b19-9d77-1e2c9a4f77aa
description: Detects path-traversal or dangerous-upload exploit requests to Adobe ColdFusion (/CFIDE/, /cf_scripts/, .cfm/.cfc) and Campaign Classic (/nl/, /nms/) endpoints patched in APSB26-68/71.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seo-poisoned-software-sites-abuse.html
  - https://helpx.adobe.com/security/security-bulletin.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/01
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1083
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_endpoint:
    cs-uri-stem|contains:
      - '/CFIDE/'
      - '/cf_scripts/'
      - '/nl/'
      - '/nms/'
      - '.cfm'
      - '.cfc'
  selection_traversal:
    cs-uri-query|contains:
      - '../'
      - '..%2f'
      - '..%252f'
      - '%2e%2e'
  condition: selection_endpoint and selection_traversal
level: high
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.http_method) as http_method values(Web.status) as status from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/CFIDE/*" OR Web.url="*/cf_scripts/*" OR Web.url="*/nl/*" OR Web.url="*/nms/*" OR Web.url="*.cfm*" OR Web.url="*.cfc*") AND (Web.url="*../*" OR Web.url="*..%2f*" OR Web.url="*..%252f*" OR Web.url="*%2e%2e*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.http_method) as http_method values(Web.status) as status from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/CFIDE/*" OR Web.url="*/cf_scripts/*" OR Web.url="*/nl/*" OR Web.url="*/nms/*" OR Web.url="*.cfm*" OR Web.url="*.cfc*") AND (Web.url="*../*" OR Web.url="*..%2f*" OR Web.url="*..%252f*" OR Web.url="*%2e%2e*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | sort - count
Adobe ColdFusion / Campaign Classic service spawning a command interpreter AIExploitation High
Detects the ColdFusion JVM/service (coldfusion.exe, cfexec.exe, jvm.exe/java.exe under the CF install path) or Campaign Classic nlserver.exe spawning cmd/powershell/wscript/certutil — the post-exploitation execution stage of the arbitrary-code-execution flaws (CVE-2026-48277/48281/48316/48282/48286). Web/app servers should almost never fork a shell, so the parent to child pair is high-signal. Rationale: Anchors on the concrete ColdFusion (coldfusion.exe/cfexec.exe/jvm/java under the CF path) and Campaign Classic (nlserver.exe) runtime binaries implied by the advisory as the RCE execution context; an app server forking a shell is the classic web-exploit tell for CVE-2026-48277/48281/48316/48282/48286. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seo-poisoned-software-sites-abuse.html • https://helpx.adobe.com/security/security-bulletin.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1203 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ColdFusion <cfexecute> tags in legitimate application code that shell out to cmd.exe
  • Scheduled ColdFusion admin tasks invoking utilities via the JVM
  • Campaign Classic delivery workflows launching helper scripts via nlserver
  • Java-based ColdFusion add-ons legitimately spawning certutil for cert operations
  • Backup/monitoring agents whose java.exe lives under an Adobe path running housekeeping shells
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("\\ColdFusion\\bin\\", "cfml.cli") or ParentCmd has "scheduled-task-runner")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture the full child command line and the parent's recent HTTP context — correlate the spawn time against W3CIISLog for a preceding traversal/upload request to the same host. Step 2 (contain): If the child downloads or executes a payload, isolate the host, kill the process tree, and snapshot the CF web root for web-shell artifacts. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all internet-facing ColdFusion/Campaign assets via DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities for the APSB26-68/71 CVEs and confirm patch level (ColdFusion 2023 U21 / 2025 U10 / ACC v7 7.4.3 build 9397).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("coldfusion.exe", "cfexec.exe", "jvm.exe", "java.exe", "nlserver.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("ColdFusion", "cfusion", "Campaign", "Adobe", "neolane")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "bitsadmin.exe", "certutil.exe", "curl.exe", "bash.exe", "sh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\coldfusion.exe", "\\cfexec.exe", "\\jvm.exe", "\\java.exe", "\\nlserver.exe")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ColdFusion", "cfusion", "Campaign", "Adobe", "neolane")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe", "\\powershell.exe", "\\pwsh.exe", "\\wscript.exe", "\\cscript.exe", "\\mshta.exe", "\\bitsadmin.exe", "\\certutil.exe", "\\curl.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Adobe ColdFusion or Campaign Classic Service Spawning Command Interpreter
id: c1a7f4b9-3e21-4d6a-8f0c-2b7e5d9a1c33
description: Detects the ColdFusion JVM/service or Campaign Classic nlserver spawning a shell/LOLBin, indicating exploitation of the APSB26-68/71 RCE flaws.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seo-poisoned-software-sites-abuse.html
  - https://helpx.adobe.com/security/security-bulletin.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/01
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1203
  - attack.t1059
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\coldfusion.exe'
      - '\cfexec.exe'
      - '\jvm.exe'
      - '\java.exe'
      - '\nlserver.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\coldfusion.exe OR *\ColdFusion.exe OR *\cfexec.exe OR *\nlserver.exe OR *\jvm.exe OR *\java.exe) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\wscript.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\mshta.exe OR *\certutil.exe OR *\CertUtil.exe OR *\bitsadmin.exe OR *\curl.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/(coldfusion|cfexec|jvm|java|nlserver)\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|bitsadmin|certutil|curl)\.exe$/i
| ParentImageFileName=/(ColdFusion|cfusion|Campaign|Adobe|neolane)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_hash) as hash from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("coldfusion.exe","cfexec.exe","jvm.exe","java.exe","nlserver.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_hash) as hash from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("coldfusion.exe","cfexec.exe","jvm.exe","java.exe","nlserver.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime
Web shell written to web root by ColdFusion / Campaign Classic runtime AIInstallation High
Detects the ColdFusion/Campaign runtime process writing a new server-executable script (.cfm/.cfml/.cfc/.jsp/.jspx/.aspx) into a web-accessible directory — the persistence foothold enabled by the unrestricted-upload-of-dangerous-file flaws CVE-2026-48276/48283. Fidelity comes from pairing the writing process (the vulnerable app server itself) with a script-file extension landing under wwwroot/CFIDE. Rationale: Ties the CVE-2026-48276/48283 'unrestricted upload of dangerous file type' primitive to its observable artifact: the CF/Campaign process itself writing a .cfm/.jsp into wwwroot/CFIDE — a combination legitimate app operation almost never produces. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seo-poisoned-software-sites-abuse.html • https://helpx.adobe.com/security/security-bulletin.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ColdFusion administrator deploying legitimate new .cfm/.cfc files via the CF admin file manager
  • Application auto-compilation writing generated .cfm templates into cache dirs overlapping web root
  • CI/CD deployment agent running as the CF service account pushing code updates
  • Campaign Classic package installs writing .jsp resources under neolane paths
  • ColdFusion 2023 U21 / 2025 U10 patch process replacing bundled .cfm files
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "\\cache\\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "deploy-agent"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the newly written file and inspect for web-shell markers (cfexecute, Runtime.exec, eval, request-param passthrough); check whether a deployment window explains it. Step 2 (contain): If malicious, quarantine the file, rotate the CF service-account and datasource credentials, isolate the host, and block HTTP GET/POST to the new path at the WAF. Step 3 (hunt): Search DeviceNetworkEvents/W3CIISLog for requests to the exact new filename (attacker interacting with the shell) and DeviceProcessEvents for child processes of the CF runtime across all ColdFusion/Campaign assets.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".cfm" or FileName endswith ".cfml" or FileName endswith ".cfc" or FileName endswith ".jsp" or FileName endswith ".jspx" or FileName endswith ".aspx"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("coldfusion.exe", "cfexec.exe", "jvm.exe", "java.exe", "nlserver.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any ("wwwroot", "CFIDE", "webroot", "neolane", "Campaign")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("cfm", "cfml", "cfc", "jsp", "jspx", "aspx")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("coldfusion.exe", "cfexec.exe", "jvm.exe", "java.exe", "nlserver.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("wwwroot", "CFIDE", "webroot", "neolane", "Campaign")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Web Shell Written to Web Root by ColdFusion or Campaign Classic Process
id: 4b8e2d17-9c05-4a3f-b1d6-7e0f3a2c88bd
description: Detects the ColdFusion/Campaign runtime writing a server-executable script into a web-accessible directory, the persistence stage of the CVE-2026-48276/48283 unrestricted-upload flaws.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seo-poisoned-software-sites-abuse.html
  - https://helpx.adobe.com/security/security-bulletin.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/01
tags:
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\coldfusion.exe'
      - '\cfexec.exe'
      - '\jvm.exe'
      - '\java.exe'
      - '\nlserver.exe'
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.cfm'
      - '.cfml'
      - '.cfc'
      - '.jsp'
      - '.jspx'
      - '.aspx'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\coldfusion.exe OR *\ColdFusion.exe OR *\cfexec.exe OR *\jvm.exe OR *\java.exe OR *\nlserver.exe) @TargetFilename:(*.cfm OR *.cfml OR *.cfc OR *.jsp OR *.jspx OR *.aspx)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\.(cfm|cfml|cfc|jsp|jspx|aspx)$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(coldfusion|cfexec|jvm|java|nlserver)\.exe$/i
| regex("(wwwroot|CFIDE|webroot|neolane|Campaign)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name IN ("coldfusion.exe","cfexec.exe","jvm.exe","java.exe","nlserver.exe")) AND (Filesystem.file_name="*.cfm" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cfml" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cfc" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.jsp" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.jspx" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.aspx") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*wwwroot*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*CFIDE*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*webroot*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*neolane*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name IN ("coldfusion.exe","cfexec.exe","jvm.exe","java.exe","nlserver.exe")) AND (Filesystem.file_name="*.cfm" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cfml" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cfc" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.jsp" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.jspx" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.aspx") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*wwwroot*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*CFIDE*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*webroot*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*neolane*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort - lastTime
Adobe ColdFusion / Campaign Classic hosts exposed to APSB26-68 CVSS 10.0 RCE CVE AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces every managed host whose software inventory maps to the maximum-severity Adobe CVEs disclosed in this advisory (ColdFusion 2023/2025 and on-premise Campaign Classic v7), so the SOC can prioritise patching to ColdFusion 2023 Update 21 / 2025 Update 10 / ACC v7 7.4.3 build 9397. Advisory states no in-the-wild exploitation yet, making proactive exposure reduction the highest-value action. Rationale: Uses the exact ten CVE IDs pre-extracted from the advisory against the TVM inventory to produce a concrete, patch-actionable exposure list — the correct primary response for an advisory with no observed intrusion. Re-emitted UC: defender_kql rewritten so the make_set/max aggregates precede a clean `by` clause with no bare projected column after `by`, fixing the prior L4 syntax error. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seo-poisoned-software-sites-abuse.html • https://helpx.adobe.com/security/security-bulletin.html
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM lag reporting a host as vulnerable minutes after the update actually landed
  • Adobe-hosted Campaign instances flagged though CVE-2026-48286 only affects on-premise deployments
  • Development/test ColdFusion instances not internet-reachable and lower priority
  • Software inventory mis-parsing a bundled JRE version as the CF product version
  • Decommissioned hosts still present in the last-seen inventory window
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareName has_any ("ColdFusion", "Campaign", "Adobe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Sort by IsInternetFacing to rank exposure; confirm each host's actual ColdFusion/Campaign build against the fixed versions (2023 U21 / 2025 U10 / ACC v7 7.4.3 build 9397). Step 2 (contain): For internet-facing unpatched hosts, apply the update immediately or place them behind WAF rules blocking traversal/upload to /CFIDE/, /cf_scripts/, /nl/ until patched; verify CVE-2026-48286 targets are truly on-premise. Step 3 (hunt): For any exposed host, run the companion UCs (interpreter spawn, web-shell write, traversal requests) retroactively over the exposure window to rule out silent pre-patch compromise.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-48276", "CVE-2026-48283", "CVE-2026-48277", "CVE-2026-48281", "CVE-2026-48316", "CVE-2026-48282", "CVE-2026-48313", "CVE-2026-48315", "CVE-2026-48307", "CVE-2026-48286")
| summarize ExposedCves = make_set(CveId), MaxSeverity = max(VulnerabilitySeverityLevel), RecommendedUpdate = any(RecommendedSecurityUpdate) by DeviceId, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, ExposedCves, MaxSeverity, RecommendedUpdate, IsInternetFacing
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-48276", "CVE-2026-48283", "CVE-2026-48277", "CVE-2026-48281", "CVE-2026-48316", "CVE-2026-48282", "CVE-2026-48313", "CVE-2026-48315", "CVE-2026-48307", "CVE-2026-48286")
| summarize ExposedCves = make_set(CveId), MaxSeverity = max(VulnerabilitySeverityLevel), RecommendedUpdate = any(RecommendedSecurityUpdate) by DeviceId, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| order by DeviceName asc
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

The Hacker News
2026-07-01 14 use cases 8 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged a new multi-stage malware delivery attack chain that uses social engineering and Blogger pages to deliver an information stealer called PureLogs. The activity has been codenamed VEIL#DROP by Securonix. It's suspected that the initial payloads are distributed either via spear-phishing or a drive-by compromise, which occurs when an unsuspecting user lands on

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] LOLBin fallback reflective .NET loading — regsvcs/installutil/msbuild/aspnet_compiler spawned by script host (VEIL#DROP) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — VEIL#DROP Malware Chain Uses Blogger Platform to Deliver PureLogs Stealer
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Anti-forensic cleanup — script-host process kill + deletion of .pdf.js dropper (VEIL#DROP) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] PowerShell/WSH beaconing to Blogger (blogspot.com) stager — VEIL#DROP
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Double-extension .pdf.js executed by Windows Script Host — VEIL#DROP initial access AIDelivery High
Hunts the VEIL#DROP entry point: a JavaScript file masquerading as a document via a double extension (e.g. transcript.pdf.js) run through wscript.exe/cscript.exe. This is the delivery lure that kicks off the PureLogs infection chain and is not covered by generic Office-spawns-script rules. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact lure shape — a .js run by WSH carrying a fake document extension (transcript.pdf.js). Double-extension + wscript/cscript execution is rare in benign traffic, making it a high-fidelity entry-point pivot independent of any single hostname. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036/007/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.007 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business apps shipping .js installers/config scripts with descriptive names containing 'pdf'
  • Admin/logon scripts stored with compound filenames
  • Software packaging tools invoking cscript against vendor .js files
  • Backup or archive utilities that name temp scripts with document-like prefixes
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","outlook.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","winrar.exe","7zFM.exe") or isempty(InitiatingProcessFileName)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full folder path and origin (FileOriginUrl/download source) of the .pdf.js and the exact command line; confirm the parent is Explorer/browser/mail client (user double-click). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the wscript/cscript tree, and quarantine the .pdf.js and any child powershell.exe. 3) Hunt: on the same host/user look for powershell.exe with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass spawned within seconds, outbound blogspot.com traffic, and LOLBin execution (regsvcs/installutil/msbuild/aspnet_compiler).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".pdf.js" or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.(pdf|docx?|xlsx?|jpe?g|png|txt|rtf)\.js\b"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".pdf.js" or CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.(pdf|docx?|xlsx?|jpe?g|png|txt|rtf)\.js\b"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Double-Extension PDF.js Script Executed by Windows Script Host (VEIL#DROP)

PowerShell/WSH beaconing to Blogger (blogspot.com) stager — VEIL#DROP AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts VEIL#DROP's abuse of Google's Blogger (blogspot.com) as a reputation-laundering stager: PowerShell or WSH reaching out to *.blogspot.com (specifically htlwub00klocate.blogspot.com) to pull the next-stage payload. Ties script-host processes to blogging-platform egress, a pairing that is almost never legitimate. Rationale: Uses the article's named stager domain (htlwub00klocate.blogspot.com) as the high-fidelity Sentinel/Splunk anchor, and the behavioural pairing of script-host processes → *.blogspot.com egress for Defender/Falcon/Datadog so the detection survives the campaign's per-execution URL mutation. Domain is currently single-sourced (Securonix); the process-context queries do not depend on it. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102/002/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user genuinely browsing a Blogger blog (but via a browser, not powershell/wscript — excluded by process filter)
  • Security tooling or RSS/feed readers implemented in PowerShell polling blogspot feeds
  • Marketing/automation scripts that legitimately post to a corporate Blogger
  • Threat-intel enrichment scripts resolving blogspot IOCs in a lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is powershell/wscript (not a browser) and capture its command line and the full RemoteUrl/redirect chain; note the number of forward slashes / mutated path. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the blogspot subdomain at proxy/DNS, and terminate the script-host process tree. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the preceding .pdf.js execution, subsequent LOLBin (regsvcs/installutil/msbuild/aspnet_compiler) launches, and PureLogs credential-store/browser-data access.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has "blogspot.com" or RemoteUrl has "htlwub00klocate"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Name has "htlwub00klocate.blogspot.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, QueryTypeName, RemoteIp
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\wscript.exe OR *\WScript.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\CScript.exe) @DestinationHostname:(*blogspot.com OR *.blogspot.com)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/blogspot\.com$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(powershell|wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*htlwub00klocate.blogspot.com" OR DNS.query="htlwub00klocate.blogspot.com") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*htlwub00klocate.blogspot.com" OR DNS.query="htlwub00klocate.blogspot.com") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Anti-forensic cleanup — script-host process kill + deletion of .pdf.js dropper (VEIL#DROP) AIInstallation High
Hunts VEIL#DROP's evidence-removal step where the PowerShell loader terminates wscript.exe and deletes the original transcript.pdf.js to minimise forensic trail. Detects deletion of a double-extension .js by a script host or PowerShell — a defense-evasion signature specific to this chain. Rationale: Combines the article's exact artifact (transcript.pdf.js, generalised to any document-masquerade .js) with the deletion action by a script host — a self-cleanup behaviour that is inherently malicious and confirms live execution rather than a dormant file. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1070/004/
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1070
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Software uninstallers removing bundled .js helper files (rarely double-extension)
  • Temp-file cleanup scripts wiping generated .js in user profiles
  • Developer tooling deleting build-artifact .js with report-like names
  • EDR/AV remediation itself deleting the quarantined dropper (check initiating process)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Quarantine")
Response runbook
1) Triage: recover the deleted file path/hash from EDR timeline and confirm the deleting process is powershell/wscript acting on a document-named .js; correlate with a prior WSH execution of the same file. 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve memory (payload runs fileless — capture before reboot). 3) Hunt: look for the wscript.exe termination event, in-memory .NET reflective loads, and blogspot.com egress on the same host to reconstruct the full chain.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileDeleted"
| where FileName endswith ".pdf.js" or FileName matches regex @"(?i)\.(pdf|docx?|xlsx?|jpe?g|png|txt|rtf)\.js$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileDeleted"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".pdf.js"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Deletion of Double-Extension .pdf.js Dropper by Script Host (VEIL#DROP)

LOLBin fallback reflective .NET loading — regsvcs/installutil/msbuild/aspnet_compiler spawned by script host (VEIL#DROP) AIExploitation High
Hunts VEIL#DROP's cascading fallback execution where the loader proxies its .NET payload through Microsoft-signed binaries (regsvcs.exe, installutil.exe, msbuild.exe, aspnet_compiler.exe) when direct in-memory execution is blocked. Detects these compiler/installer LOLBins spawned by PowerShell/WSH — an abnormal parentage that is the hallmark of this chain. Rationale: Uses the article's explicitly named fallback LOLBins and the cascading-execution model. These signed .NET utilities being spawned by a script host / PowerShell (rather than a build agent or installer) is a strong, low-ambiguity indicator of the VEIL#DROP reflective-loading fallback. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1127/001/ • https://lolbas-project.github.io/
ATT&CKT1218 T1127.001 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer workstations running MSBuild from a PowerShell/cmd build script (Visual Studio devs)
  • CI/CD or packaging automation invoking msbuild/installutil via scripted steps
  • aspnet_compiler.exe run during legitimate web-app precompilation from a deploy script
  • installutil.exe used by admins to (un)install .NET Windows services from cmd
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)" and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\azure-pipelines","\\Jenkins","\\actions-runner","\\TeamCity"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the LOLBin command line for a project/assembly path in a user-writable/temp location and confirm the parent is an interactive script host rather than a build/deploy pipeline. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the LOLBin and its script-host parent, and capture memory (the .NET assembly loads reflectively). 3) Hunt: correlate with preceding .pdf.js execution, blogspot.com egress, and wscript.exe termination on the same host; sweep the fleet for the same rare parent→LOLBin pairing.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("regsvcs.exe","installutil.exe","msbuild.exe","aspnet_compiler.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","cmd.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("regsvcs.exe","installutil.exe","msbuild.exe","aspnet_compiler.exe")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","cmd.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

logsource:
    category: process_creation

detection:

            - '\wscript.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

SecurityEvent

| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:

      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

CloudAppEvents

| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ousaban persistence via 'Financeiro' Run key AIInstallation High
Hunts the Ousaban/Javali banking trojan's persistence: a HKCU/HKLM ...\CurrentVersion\Run value named 'Financeiro' (Portuguese for 'finance') added so the payload starts with Windows. This value name is a fixed Ousaban artifact, not a generic Run-key hunt. Rationale: Anchors on the fixed Ousaban artifact — a Run value named 'Financeiro' — reported by FortiGuard and consistent with the family's documented registry persistence. The exact value name makes this far higher fidelity than a generic Run-key hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ousaban-banking-trojan-targets-iberian.html • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.ousaban • https://www.welivesecurity.com/2021/05/05/ousaban-private-photo-collection-hidden-cabinet/
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Iberian/Brazilian ERP or accounting software (a legitimate 'financeiro' module) registering its own autostart entry
  • In-house line-of-business finance app installer using Portuguese naming and a Run key
  • SCCM/Intune deploying a finance-dashboard launcher to the Run key
  • Sysadmin scripting a scheduled finance-report tool via Run
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith @"C:\Program Files" and isnotempty(InitiatingProcessSHA256)) and not (RegistryValueData has @"\Program Files")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read RegistryValueData — Ousaban points it at C:\SysMain_5874288 or another odd non-Program-Files path with an unsigned binary; a signed vendor path under Program Files is likely benign. Check InitiatingProcess (script host writing the key is a strong TP signal). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the referenced binary, delete the Run value, and force a banking-credential reset for the user given the trojan's session-hijack capability. 3) Hunt: pivot on the referenced binary's folder for FileCreated events and outbound public connections; sweep other hosts for the same value name.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "Financeiro"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValue =~ "Financeiro"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ousaban payload staging in C:\SysMain_5874288 AIInstallation High
Hunts file creation under the hardcoded Ousaban staging directory C:\SysMain_5874288, where the loader script drops the steganographic image, the embedded ZIP, and the unpacked trojan binary. The suffixed folder name masquerades as the Windows SysMain service but is a fixed campaign artifact. Rationale: C:\SysMain_5874288 is a fixed, article-named staging path with a random numeric suffix — legitimate Windows SysMain is a service, never a top-level folder with that suffix — so any file write there is high-confidence Ousaban activity (steganographic image + ZIP + unpacked binary). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ousaban-banking-trojan-targets-iberian.html • https://www.netskope.com/blog/ousaban-latam-banking-malware-abusing-cloud-services • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.ousaban
ATT&CKT1027.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A third-party app coincidentally creating a C:\SysMain* root folder (extremely unlikely with the exact _5874288 suffix)
  • Security/EDR tool quarantining or copying a sample into an analysis path under C:\
  • Backup or migration tooling restoring files to an unusual C:\ root directory
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","CSFalconService.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate files under C:\SysMain_5874288 — expect an image posing as a PDF icon, a ZIP, a loader script, and an unpacked EXE. Capture SHA256s and check the InitiatingProcess (script host download is a strong TP). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any process running from that folder, and preserve the directory before the trojan's self-delete cleanup removes the image/ZIP/script. 3) Hunt: pivot on the dropped EXE's hash across the fleet, check for the 'Financeiro' Run key on the same host, and review outbound public connections from that folder.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath startswith @"C:\SysMain_5874288"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath startswith @"C:\SysMain_5874288"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ousaban C2 egress from SysMain_5874288 binary AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound public network connections initiated by any process running from the Ousaban staging directory C:\SysMain_5874288. Anchors C2 detection on the article-specific drop path rather than the daily-rotating date-derived C2 address (which is undetectable by static IOC) or the Fortinet-flagged decoy server. Rationale: The article's daily date+secret DGA and the Fortinet-flagged decoy IP 162.33.179.46 make static network IOCs low-value; anchoring on outbound public traffic from the fixed C:\SysMain_5874288 drop path is the durable, campaign-specific C2 pivot. Sentinel left empty because this tenant's Sentinel schema lacks a process-folder-anchored network table (ImNetworkSession carries no initiating-process path). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ousaban-banking-trojan-targets-iberian.html • https://www.netskope.com/blog/ousaban-latam-banking-malware-abusing-cloud-services
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign portable app legitimately installed under a C:\SysMain* path making update checks (unlikely given the random suffix)
  • Security tooling detonating a sample from that folder in place and generating its own network traffic
  • Analyst/IR activity copying and running tools from the staging path during triage
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating binary lives in C:\SysMain_5874288 and correlate to the 'Financeiro' Run key / staging-drop UCs on the same host; note the destination IP/URL for blocking. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the observed C2 destination at the egress proxy/firewall, and reset the user's banking credentials given the trojan's remote-control and session-hijack capability. 3) Hunt: since the real C2 rotates daily via a date-derived address, hunt for the same process-folder egress across all hosts rather than the single IP, and review proxy logs for the Google-page/Pastebin config-retrieval fetches.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith @"C:\SysMain_5874288"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10), URLs=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith @"C:\SysMain_5874288"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10), URLs=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
